episode.title: Even higher diesel prices are coming
episode.description:
The average cost of a gallon of diesel was $5.68 on Wednesday — just 13 cents shy of a record high. Tariffs and ongoing wars are both to blame. But so is a seasonal upswing that happens every fall. In this episode, why diesel prices are likely going to get even steeper before they cool off. Plus: A computer model helps make the case for fewer mandated parking spots in city construction projects, Uber wants to shrink its middle management, and Alaska families celebrate dipnetting season.


Every story has an economic angle. Want some in your inbox? Subscribe to our daily or weekly newsletter.


Marketplace is more than a radio show. Check out our original reporting and financial literacy content at marketplace.org — and consider making an investment in our future.


Read the stories in today’s episode:


  • Why high diesel prices are coming at a particularly bad time
  • What it takes to reopen 19 months after a wildfire
  • Uber lays off 10% of their workforce to make the company "simpler and faster"
  • To spur more housing construction, Denver changed its parking rules

utterances.text: Uber announced today it's cutting 10% of its workforce—comes to about 3,300 jobs. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said he wants to create a simpler, leaner organization with, in particular, fewer layers of management. utterances.speaker: H

utterances.speaker: D

utterances.speaker: H
utterances.text: Sutton, who's a professor emeritus at Stanford, says the idea with cutting management layers is you get rid of the people who slow things down and battle with others for power. But sometimes it can be hard to know the unappreciated, invisible work that middle managers do.

utterances.speaker: D

utterances.speaker: H
utterances.text: Sutton says this is part of a larger trend—let go of some managers, give others bigger teams. According to a Gallup review of US workplaces, the average team has 12 people. That's about 50% larger than back in 2013. But Sutton says you can end up with teams that are too big.

utterances.speaker: D
utterances.text: What happens is that the boss gets overloaded. They become a bottleneck. It becomes frustrating.

utterances.speaker: H
utterances.text: And more decisions can end up with the big boss, says Julia Dahr with Boston Consulting Group.

utterances.speaker: K

utterances.speaker: H
utterances.text: Dahr says that shrinking an organization's size doesn't necessarily save money long term. In order for it to make sense, companies have to figure out exactly how all the work, visible and invisible, is going to get done.

utterances.speaker: K
